# Introduction

You have now met most of the families of method this course covers, and
tomorrow adds the last one. This session puts them side by side and asks the
question you will actually face when you go back to your own work: given this
model and this data, which one do I reach for?

There is no algorithm for the answer. But the choice is much less open than it
looks, because two properties of your problem rule most of the options out
before you start.

# The two questions that decide it

::: {.callout-important}
1. **Can you write down and evaluate $p(\text{data} \mid \theta)$?**
2. **Can you differentiate it?**
:::

Everything else is detail. The first question separates likelihood-based methods
from simulation-based ones. The second separates gradient-based samplers from
everything else, and it is the question people most often fail to ask before
choosing a tool.

A deterministic model with a parametric observation model answers yes to both,
which is why the [introduction](introduction.qmd) and [MCMC](mcmc.qmd) sessions
could go straight to NUTS. A stochastic model answers no to the first, because
the likelihood involves an integral over every trajectory the model could have
taken, which is what sent us to [particle filters](particle_filters.qmd). A model
you can only simulate answers no to both, which is where
[ABC](observation_models.qmd) comes in tomorrow morning.

# The methods, side by side

| Method | Needs | Cost | Reach for it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Grid search** | likelihood | hopeless beyond 2-3 parameters | you want to *see* the posterior |
| **Metropolis-Hastings** | likelihood | cheap per step, many steps | the model is small, or you need to understand what a sampler does |
| **RAM / adaptive MH** | likelihood | as MH, tunes itself | MH mixes badly and you cannot differentiate |
| **NUTS** | likelihood **and gradient** | expensive per step, few steps | you can differentiate: almost always the default |
| **Particle filter + PMMH** | simulator of a stochastic model | very expensive | the state is stochastic and you need the parameters |
| **ABC** *(tomorrow)* | simulator only | expensive, and approximate | you cannot write a likelihood at all |
| **Variational inference** | likelihood and gradient | fast | you need an answer in seconds and can accept bias |

::: {.callout-warning}
The table reads top to bottom as increasing generality, and generality is not
free. Every step down it buys you the ability to handle a harder model by
spending more computation, accepting more approximation, or both. Do not take a
step you do not need: fitting a deterministic model with ABC is not wrong, it is
merely thousands of times slower than fitting it with NUTS and less accurate.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise: match the problem to the method"}
For each of these, decide which method you would try first and, more
importantly, why the ones above it in the table will not do.

1. An SEIR model fitted to weekly case counts, five parameters, deterministic.
2. The same model, but the transmission rate is a random walk over 100 weeks.
3. An individual-based simulation of household transmission, where the
   likelihood would require summing over every possible chain of infection.
4. A deterministic model you need to refit every hour as new data arrive.
5. A stochastic compartmental model with six parameters and a small population,
   where demographic noise genuinely matters.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
1. NUTS. Deterministic, few parameters, differentiable.
2. Still NUTS, but the 100 random-walk increments are parameters too, so this is
   a 105-dimensional problem and the AD backend becomes a real decision. See
   [Beyond Turing](julia_ecosystem.qmd) on forward versus reverse mode.
3. ABC, or a synthetic likelihood. You can simulate households easily and cannot
   write the likelihood at all. This is tomorrow's session.
4. Variational inference, if you can tolerate the bias, and NUTS if you can
   afford it. This is the one case where "fast and slightly wrong" beats "slow
   and right", because an answer after the decision is worth nothing.
5. Particle MCMC. The state is stochastic, so the likelihood needs marginalising
   over trajectories, which is exactly what the particle filter estimates.
:::

# What actually goes wrong

In practice the method is rarely the thing that fails. Four other things are.

**The observation model.** A Poisson likelihood on overdispersed data makes the
posterior far too confident and lets one bad day dominate the fit, as the
[observation models session](observation_models.qmd) showed. This is the most
common real failure, and no amount of sampler sophistication rescues it.

**The priors.** Vague priors are not neutral. A `Uniform(1, 20)` on $R_0$ says a
value of 19 is as plausible as 2, and prior predictive checks turn that from an
abstraction into a picture of epidemics that infect everyone in four days.

**Identifiability.** If two parameters trade off against each other, no sampler
will separate them, and a well-mixed chain will happily report a confident
posterior along the ridge. The [diagnostics session](mcmc_diagnostics.qmd) is
about noticing this.

**The model.** A model that cannot produce the data you observed will not be
saved by better inference. Posterior predictive checks are how you find out.

::: {.callout-important}
Sampler problems announce themselves: R̂, divergences, terrible trace plots.
Model problems do not. A converged chain from a bad model looks exactly like a
converged chain from a good one, which is why
[model checking](model_checking.qmd) is a separate discipline from diagnostics.
:::

# Beyond this course

The methods here are the working set, and there are two directions people
commonly go next.

**Scale.** Fitting many models, or one model to many regions, means parallel
chains, GPUs, and tools built for it. The Julia stack is well placed here:
`sample(model, NUTS(), MCMCThreads(), n, n_chains)` is the entire change needed
to run chains in parallel, and the [wider ecosystem](julia_ecosystem.qmd)
session covers sampling outside Turing when you need it.

**Structure.** Real surveillance data arrives late, incompletely, and through
several different streams at once. Reporting delays, nowcasting and multi-source
evidence synthesis all sit on top of what you have learned rather than replacing
it: the model gets more elaborate, the inference machinery stays the same.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise: your own problem"}
Take a model you actually want to fit.

1. Can you write down $p(\text{data} \mid \theta)$? If not, what is stopping you:
   a stochastic state, an intractable sum, or a simulator you did not write?
2. Can you differentiate it? If the model calls out to code you cannot
   differentiate through, that rules out NUTS regardless of everything else.
3. Which row of the table does that leave you on?
4. What would you check first if the answer looked wrong?

If you have time, discuss it with the person next to you. Question 4 is usually
the one that changes people's plans.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Learning points"}

- Two questions decide most of it: can you evaluate the likelihood, and can you
  differentiate it
- Generality costs computation and accuracy, so take the most specific method
  your problem allows
- The observation model, the priors and identifiability cause more real failures
  than the choice of sampler
- Sampler problems are loud and model problems are silent, which is why
  diagnostics and model checking are separate jobs

:::
